title: Given a grid of characters and a set of dictionary words, find all dictionary words that can be formed by a path of adjacent cells without reusing a cell. Explain how the Trie pattern accelerates the search, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Word Search with a Trie (Find Which Dictionary Words Appear in a Character Grid)

s1_definition.profdef: Word Search with a Trie combines a backtracking grid traversal with the Trie pattern. We load all dictionary words into a trie, then run a depth-first search from every cell, descending the trie by the current character. When we land on a trie node marked as a word we record it. The trie lets us explore all words simultaneously and prune the moment no word shares the current prefix.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a grid of characters pulled from a scanned cheque region to spot any known keyword like SALARY or RENT appearing along connected cells. A trie of the keywords lets the scan follow all keywords at once and stop early on dead ends.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the grid and the trie together, pruning any path whose prefix matches no word.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Search with a Trie combines a backtracking grid traversal with the Trie pattern. We load all dictionary words into a trie, then run a depth-first search from every cell, descending the trie by the current character. When we land on a trie node marked as a word we record it. The trie lets us explore all words simultaneously and prune the moment no word shares the current prefix.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a grid of characters pulled from a scanned cheque region to spot any known keyword like SALARY or RENT appearing along connected cells. A trie of the keywords lets the scan follow all keywords at once and stop early on dead ends.

**One line to remember:** Walk the grid and the trie together, pruning any path whose prefix matches no word.

sections.s2_technical:
We build a trie from all target words so that every prefix is represented. Then from each grid cell we start a depth-first search that carries the current trie node. At a cell we first check that the trie node has a child for the cell's character, and if not we prune immediately because no word continues with this prefix. If it does, we descend to that child, and if that child is marked as a word we record the word. We mark the cell visited, recurse into the four adjacent cells, then unmark the cell on the way back so other paths can reuse it.

The search core is `void dfs(r, c, node) { char ch = grid[r][c]; TrieNode child = node.children.get(ch); if (child == null) return; if (child.word != null) found.add(child.word); char save = grid[r][c]; grid[r][c] = '#'; for each neighbour dfs(nr, nc, child); grid[r][c] = save; }`. Storing the full word on the terminal node avoids rebuilding it. A concrete check: a grid containing S, A, L, A, R, Y along a connected path reports SALARY. Senior nuance: the trie turns many separate word searches into one shared traversal, pruning dead prefixes early, and marking the cell during recursion enforces the no-reuse rule.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India scans a small grid of characters extracted from a cheque region and wants to detect any known keyword such as SALARY or RENT formed along connected cells, because spotting such keywords helps classify the cheque. Searching each keyword separately across the grid is wasteful. This is exactly how Word Search with a Trie works: it loads the keywords into a trie and runs one shared backtracking search that prunes dead prefixes.

The code defines a `GridKeywordService` with `findKeywords(grid, words)`, plus a `TrieNode`. A `Demo` builds a small grid and keyword set and logs the keywords found.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a three by three grid and the keyword set SAL, RENT, RAT. We want every keyword formed along connected cells.

Step 1 — We build the trie from the keywords, so the root branches into S for SAL and R for RENT and RAT, sharing the R branch.

Step 2 — Starting the search at the top-left S, the trie has a child for S, so we descend, then the neighbour A has a child, then the neighbour L has a child marked as the word SAL, so we record SAL.

Step 3 — Starting at the centre R, the trie descends, then A to the right has a child, then T below A has a child marked as the word RAT, so we record RAT.

Step 4 — Still from the R branch, following R then E then N then T along connected cells reaches the node marked as the word RENT, so we record RENT.

Step 5 — Any path whose prefix matches no keyword is pruned immediately, so the found list is SAL, RAT, RENT in discovery order. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:59:50 PM com.bank.gridkw.service.GridKeywordService findKeywords
INFO: Keywords found in grid = [SAL, RAT, RENT]
Oct 27, 2026 9:59:50 PM com.bank.gridkw.GridKeywordApplication main
INFO: Detected cheque keywords: [SAL, RAT, RENT]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Build trie from {SAL, RENT, RAT}
    │ root → S→A→L(word SAL)
    │ root → R→E→N→T(word RENT)
    │ root → R→A→T(word RAT)   (shares R)
    ▼
  DFS each grid cell carrying a trie node
    │ no child for char → prune
    │ child.word != null → record word
    │ mark '#', recurse 4 neighbours, restore
    ▼
  Output: [SAL, RAT, RENT]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search with a Trie marries a backtracking grid traversal with the Trie pattern, and the reason the trie matters is that it lets me search for every dictionary word at the same time instead of once per word. I first load all the words into a trie so that every prefix is represented, then I launch a depth-first search from each grid cell, and crucially each search frame carries the current trie node alongside the grid position.

At every cell I check whether the current trie node has a child for the cell's character. If it does not, I prune that path immediately because no word continues with this prefix, which is exactly where the trie saves work. If it does, I descend into that child, and if the child is marked as a complete word I record it. I mark the cell visited so the path cannot reuse it, recurse into the four neighbours, and then restore the cell on the way back so other paths are free to use it.

At the National Bank of India I used this to scan a small grid of characters extracted from a cheque region for known keywords like SALARY and RENT formed along connected cells, which helped classify the cheque. I loaded the keywords into a trie and ran one shared backtracking search. Explaining that the trie drives the traversal, that a missing child prunes the path early, and that marking and restoring the cell enforces the no-reuse rule is what shows an interviewer I understand this combined application of the Trie pattern.
